back2basics.concept: Right to Speedy Trial and Bail
back2basics.text: The right to a speedy trial is a facet of the fundamental right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution. Bail is a legal mechanism allowing temporary release of an accused pending trial, balancing individual liberty and public interest. Courts consider factors like severity of the offence, criminal antecedents, and societal safety when granting bail.

2026-11-24-pm-0820d2febb.deck: The Supreme Court ruled that a criminal with previous convictions cannot be granted bail only on the basis of the right to a speedy trial. This judgment clarifies the balance between individual rights and societal interests in criminal justice, a key topic for UPSC exams.

back2basics.concept: UN Climate Change Conferences and Consensus Decision-Making
back2basics.text: The UN Climate Change Conferences (COP) are annual meetings where countries negotiate global climate action under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Decisions require consensus, meaning all parties must agree, which can stall agreements if key countries disagree. The cover text is a political document summarizing the conference outcome and frames future climate commitments.

2026-11-24-pm-37a12f0de9.deck: COP31 in Turkiye failed to reach consensus on a climate deal due to disagreements over fossil fuel phase-out language. This outcome highlights challenges in global climate negotiations and India's stance on balancing climate ambition with development needs.

body.label: Fossil fuel phase-out dispute
body.text: The European Union and about 130 countries rejected the COP31 President’s draft cover text because it did not include explicit language on phasing out fossil fuels, which they saw as essential to meet climate goals.

body.label: Opposing positions
body.text: India, China, and Saudi Arabia supported the draft text, opposing prescriptive fossil fuel targets, emphasizing the need for nationally determined, just, and equitable energy transitions backed by finance and technology.

body.label: Consensus requirement
body.text: The UN climate talks require unanimous agreement on the cover text, so the EU-led rejection prevented any consensus deal despite the conference running 48 hours overtime.

sections.heading: Why did COP31 fail to reach a climate agreement?

body.label: India’s climate diplomacy stance
body.text: India stressed that climate ambition must be matched with means of implementation, including finance, technology, and capacity-building, reflecting its development priorities alongside climate action.

body.label: Support for fossil fuel use
body.text: India is part of the Like Minded Developing Countries coalition that insists on continued fossil fuel use in the foreseeable future to support economic growth while also deploying renewable energy.

body.label: Focus on equity and responsibility
body.text: India and its allies expressed concern that the draft text diluted principles of equity and common but differentiated responsibilities, and did not adequately reflect developed countries’ historical emissions.

sections.heading: What are the implications of the COP31 outcome for India?

body.label: Science and ambition gap
body.text: The EU and others argued the draft decision fell short of scientific requirements to keep global warming below 1.5°C and risked widening the gap between commitments and action.

body.label: Equity concerns
body.text: Developing countries like Panama criticized the text for weakening previous commitments and relying too much on technologies like carbon capture instead of deep systemic changes.

body.label: Challenge of multilateralism
body.text: COP31 exposed the difficulty of achieving global climate action when parties have divergent development needs and priorities, especially regarding fossil fuel dependency.

back2basics.text: Judicial review allows courts to examine the legality and constitutionality of decisions, including those affecting religious practices. Courts often balance the protection of religious customs with statutory laws and public order, ensuring that no permanent rights are granted without proper legal basis. Review petitions are a legal mechanism to challenge Supreme Court orders but require strong grounds such as factual errors or legal oversights.

back2basics.text: Transboundary river water sharing treaties are agreements between countries sharing rivers to allocate water equitably, manage disputes, and ensure sustainable use. They often include mechanisms for data sharing, joint monitoring, and emergency consultations to address variability in water flow. Such treaties are crucial for maintaining peaceful relations and cooperation between riparian states.

2026-11-24-pm-c2db131c66.deck: The 30-year-old Ganga Water Treaty between India and Bangladesh is set to lapse on December 12, 2026, with ongoing discussions about its renewal. Understanding the treaty’s provisions, challenges, and current negotiation stances is crucial for grasping India’s water diplomacy and regional cooperation with Bangladesh.

mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because the treaty does not guarantee a minimum water release regardless of flow; it only has guaranteed releases in alternate periods and an emergency consultation clause.

body.label: Origins of dispute
body.text: Tensions over Ganga water sharing began in the 1950s with India’s construction of the Farakka barrage to divert water to the Hooghly river, causing concerns in Bangladesh over reduced flow and desertification.

body.label: Treaty formation
body.text: After several ad hoc agreements failed, India and Bangladesh signed the Ganga Water Treaty in December 1996 to create a 30-year framework for sharing dry-season water flows and to establish a joint committee for monitoring.

sections.heading: What is the history and purpose of the Ganga Water Treaty?

body.label: Flow-based sharing
body.text: The treaty sets a three-tiered water allocation system based on 10-day average flows at Farakka: equal sharing if flow is ≤70,000 cusecs; Bangladesh gets 35,000 cusecs if flow is 70,000–75,000 cusecs; and India gets 40,000 cusecs if flow is ≥75,000 cusecs.

body.label: Guaranteed releases
body.text: Between March 11 and May 10, both countries receive guaranteed 35,000 cusecs in alternate 10-day periods, though the treaty lacks a minimum guaranteed flow clause.

body.label: Emergency clause
body.text: If flow falls below 50,000 cusecs, both governments must consult immediately to adjust sharing based on equity and no harm principles.

body.label: Dispute resolution
body.text: A Joint Committee with equal representatives manages implementation and disputes, with unresolved issues referred to the Joint Rivers Commission overseeing 54 shared rivers.

sections.heading: What are the key provisions of the 1996 treaty?

body.label: Criticism of treaty adequacy
body.text: The treaty is criticised for not addressing future population growth and climate change impacts on water availability.

body.label: India’s demands
body.text: India reportedly seeks an additional 30,000 to 35,000 cusecs during the March 11-May 10 period and a shorter renewal duration of 10 to 15 years.

body.label: Bangladesh’s demands
body.text: Bangladesh requests a guaranteed 40,000 cusecs release between February and May, reinstatement of a minimum guarantee clause from a 1977 agreement, longer renewal periods, and enhanced flood data sharing.

body.label: Points of contention
body.text: India opposes Bangladesh’s fixed volumetric minimum guarantee demand due to the asymmetric hydrological risk it imposes on upstream India, especially amid climate variability.

body.label: Political and regional context
body.text: Tensions over political issues like former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s extradition and Bihar’s opposition to the treaty renewal add complexity to negotiations.

sections.heading: What are the current challenges and negotiation positions?

body.label: Bilateral water diplomacy
body.text: The treaty renewal is a test of cooperative water management and regional diplomacy between India and Bangladesh.

body.label: Institutional strengthening
body.text: Experts suggest the renewal offers an opportunity to build resilient transboundary water institutions addressing sharing, data, dispute resolution, and risk management.

body.label: Strategic regional vision
body.text: Renewal could reimagine regional cooperation amid shared vulnerabilities and a fragmented global economy, requiring reinvestment in political capital and bilateral mechanisms.

back2basics.text: The Kartarpur Corridor is a visa-free border crossing that connects the Sikh holy site of Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Pakistan to Gurdwara Dera Baba Nanak in India. It was created to facilitate Sikh pilgrims visiting the sacred site without requiring a visa, promoting religious tourism and cultural ties between India and Pakistan. back2basics.concept: Juvenile Justice Act and Children’s Courts
back2basics.text: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act provides a legal framework for handling offences involving children. Children’s Courts are specialized courts designated to try offences under this Act, ensuring child-sensitive procedures and protections. The 2022 amendment mandated that all offences under the Act be tried exclusively by Children’s Courts, centralizing jurisdiction to better protect child rights.

2026-11-24-pm-eef9af3718.deck: The Delhi High Court ruled on November 23, 2026, that all pending cases under the Juvenile Justice Act must be tried in Children’s Courts, even if trials began before the 2022 amendment. This clarifies procedural jurisdiction and safeguards child rights, relevant for understanding juvenile justice reforms and court procedures.

body.label: Mandatory Children’s Courts
body.text: The Court ruled that all cases involving offences under the Juvenile Justice Act must be tried by Children’s Courts, including those pending before other courts when the law was amended in 2022.

body.label: Retrospective application
body.text: The Court held that the change in trial forum is procedural and thus the 2022 amendment mandating Children’s Courts applies retrospectively.

sections.heading: What did the Delhi High Court rule about Juvenile Justice Act cases?

body.label: No automatic transfer
body.text: The Court clarified that only offences under the Juvenile Justice Act must be tried in Children’s Courts; ordinary criminal cases with minor victims do not require transfer.

sections.heading: Does every case with a minor victim go to Children’s Court?

body.label: Change in appeal forum
body.text: Since the trial forum changes to Children’s Courts, appeals will now lie before the High Court instead of the Court of Sessions.

body.label: No impact on rights
body.text: The Court noted that this procedural change does not affect the accused’s or State’s rights to appeal.

sections.heading: How does this ruling affect appeals and trial rights?
